facts.statement: The genus Scansoriopteryx was described by Czerkas and Yuan in 2002.
facts.quote: parent_authority: Czerkas & Yuan, 2002

facts.statement: Scansoriopteryx is known from a single juvenile fossil specimen discovered in Liaoning, China.
facts.quote: Described from only a single juvenile fossil specimen found in Liaoning, China

facts.statement: The known specimen of Scansoriopteryx is sparrow-sized.
facts.quote: Scansoriopteryx is a sparrow-sized animal

facts.statement: Scansoriopteryx had an unusual, elongated third finger that may have supported a membranous wing.
facts.quote: It possessed an unusual, elongated third finger which may have supported a membranous wing

facts.statement: Fossilized impressions of feathers are preserved on the type specimen of Scansoriopteryx.
facts.quote: The type specimen of Scansoriopteryx also contains the fossilized impression of feathers.

facts.statement: Most researchers consider the genus Scansoriopteryx to be a synonym of Epidendrosaurus.
facts.quote: Most researchers regard this genus as a synonym of Epidendrosaurus

facts.statement: The fossil range of Scansoriopteryx spans from the Callovian to the Oxfordian stages.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Callovian to Oxfordian,

facts.statement: Czerkas and Yuan initially reported that the Scansoriopteryx specimen likely came from the Yixian Formation.
facts.quote: Czerkas and Yuan initially reported that it had likely come from the Yixian Formation

facts.statement: The age of the Daohugou Beds, where related fossils are found, is supposedly mid-late Jurassic but is hotly contested.
facts.quote: The Daohugou Beds supposedly date to the mid-late Jurassic Period, but this is hotly contested.

facts.statement: The type specimen of Scansoriopteryx heilmanni represents the remains of a hatchling maniraptoran dinosaur.
facts.quote: The type specimen of Scansoriopteryx heilmanni (specimen number CAGS02-IG-gausa-1/DM 607) represents the fossilized remains of a hatchling maniraptoran dinosaur

facts.statement: The lower jaw of Scansoriopteryx contained at least twelve teeth, which were larger at the front than at the back.
facts.quote: The lower jaw contained at least twelve teeth, larger in the front of the jaws than in the back.

facts.statement: Long wing feathers on Scansoriopteryx appear to attach to the elongated third digit rather than the middle digit.
facts.quote: The long wing feathers, or remiges, appear to attach to this long digit instead of the middle digit as in birds and other maniraptorans.

facts.statement: Scansoriopteryx had a pubis that pointed forward, a primitive trait among theropods.
facts.quote: It also had a pubis (hip bone) which pointed forward, a primitive trait among theropods

facts.statement: Scansoriopteryx had short legs with small pebbly scales and possible impressions of long feathers on the upper foot.
facts.quote: The legs were short, and preserve small pebbly scales along the upper foot (metatarsus), as well as possible impressions of long feathers in the same area

facts.statement: Scansoriopteryx had an unusually large first toe that may have been reversed to allow grasping.
facts.quote: It also had an unusually large first toe, or hallux, which was low on the foot and may have been reversed, allowing some grasping ability.

facts.statement: Unlike modern bird hatchlings, Scansoriopteryx had forelimbs longer than its hind limbs.
facts.quote: They noted that, unlike all modern bird hatchlings, the forelimbs of Scansoriopteryx are longer than the hind limbs.

facts.statement: Czerkas and Yuan interpreted the hallux of Scansoriopteryx as reversed, a condition common in modern tree-dwelling birds.
facts.quote: The authors interpreted the hallux as reversed, the condition of a backward-pointing toe being widespread among modern tree-dwelling birds.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Scansoriopteryx may have used its tail as a prop, similar to modern woodpeckers.
facts.quote: The tail may have been used as a prop, much like the tails of modern woodpeckers.

facts.statement: Fossils of Scansoriopteryx preserve wispy, down-like feathers forming V-shaped patterns similar to modern down feathers.
facts.quote: Scansoriopteryx fossils preserve impressions of wispy, down-like feathers around select parts of the body, forming V-shaped patterns similar to those seen in modern down feathers.

facts.statement: Czerkas and Yuan speculated that adults may have had wing feathers for leaping or gliding, but ruled out powered flight.
facts.quote: The longer feathers in this region led Czerkas and Yuan to speculate that adult scansoriopterygids may have had reasonably well-developed wing feathers which could have aided in leaping or rudimentary gliding, though they ruled out the possibility that Scansoriopteryx could have achieved powered flight.

facts.statement: Scansoriopteryx had a semilunate bone in the wrist allowing for bird-like folding motion in the hand.
facts.quote: Like other maniraptorans, Scansoriopteryx had a semilunate (half-moon shaped) bone in the wrist that allowed for bird-like folding motion in the hand.

facts.statement: The holotype skeleton of Epidendrosaurus was recovered from the Daohugou fossil beds in northeastern China.
facts.quote: The holotype skeleton of Epidendrosaurus was recovered from the Daohugou fossil beds of northeastern China.

facts.statement: The age of the Daohugou beds has been estimated anywhere from 169 million years ago in the Middle Jurassic to 122 million years ago in the Early Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Various papers have placed the fossils here anywhere from the Middle Jurassic period (169 million years ago) to the Early Cretaceous period (122 ma).

facts.statement: The exact age of the Daohugou formation is debated because it affects understanding of Epidendrosaurus relationships and the origin of birds.
facts.quote: The age of this formation has implications for the relationship between Epidendrosaurus and similar dinosaurs, as well as for the origin of birds in general.

facts.statement: Scansoriopteryx is classified as a member of the clade Avialae and is considered a close relative of true birds.
facts.quote: Studies of dinosaur relationships have found Scansoriopteryx to be a close relative of true birds and a member of the clade Avialae.

facts.statement: The genus Scansoriopteryx gave its name to the family Scansoriopterygidae.
facts.quote: Scansoriopteryx lent its name to the family Scansoriopterygidae.

facts.statement: There is a scientific debate regarding whether Scansoriopteryx is a senior synonym or a junior synonym of the genus Epidendrosaurus.
facts.quote: In scientific literature, the genus Scansoriopteryx has been treated as a senior synonym of Epidendrosaurus by some scientists, such as Alan Feduccia, and as a junior synonym by others such as Thomas R. Holtz, Jr. and Kevin Padian.

facts.statement: The hypothesis that Scansoriopteryx evolved from non-dinosaurian archosaurs rather than being a dinosaur has been overwhelmingly rejected by paleontologists.
facts.quote: This conclusion has been overwhelmingly rejected by other paleontologists due to the clear morphological similarities scansoriopterygids have to other maniraptoran dinosaurs.

facts.statement: Scansoriopteryx lived during the Barremian to Aptian stages, between 125.77 and 119.57 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Barremian to Aptian (125.77 to 119.57 million years ago)

facts.statement: The genus Scansoriopteryx was named by Czerkas and Yuan in 2002.
facts.quote: PBDB name: Scansoriopteryx (genus), Czerkas and Yuan 2002

facts.statement: Researchers Czerkas and Yuan argued that Scansoriopteryx possessed primitive and birdlike characters that supported an unorthodox interpretation of dinosaur evolution.
facts.quote: Czerkas and Yuan used the suite of primitive and birdlike characters in Scansoriopteryx to argue for an unorthodox interpretation of dinosaur evolution.
